# The Annotated Archive

A shoebox of photographs is not an archive. It is only potential—one that dies with whoever last remembered what was inside it. The difference between a collection of objects and a family archive is annotation, and annotation is a form of labor that most families never quite get around to performing.

Consider a photograph I know of, the kind that exists in nearly every family: a woman standing in a kitchen, caught mid-turn, holding a dish towel. Without explanation, it is almost nothing—a posed nothing, even, since she clearly did not know the picture was being taken. But when my grandmother finally wrote on the back, decades later, the image became dense with information. The kitchen was in a rented apartment on the far side of town, not the house everyone associated with her. The year was 1958, which meant she was pregnant with her first child. And the dish towel, she noted, was one she had embroidered herself because she couldn't afford to buy linens. Three sentences on the back of a photograph transformed an anonymous domestic scene into a document
